name: ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge)
description: A new question set, text corpus, and baselines assembled to encourage AI research in advanced question answering. The ARC Dataset consists of 7,787 natural, grade-school science questions authored for standardized tests, partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set. The release also includes the ARC Corpus of 14M science-related sentences and baseline neural models.
creator: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord
citeAs: Clark, Peter; Cowhey, Isaac; Etzioni, Oren; Khot, Tushar; Sabharwal, Ashish; Schoenick, Carissa; Tafjord, Oyvind. Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. arXiv:1803.05457v1, 2018.
rai:dataCollection: The ARC dataset was assembled through several months of extensive search and investigation to obtain publicly releasable natural science questions authored for standardized tests. The dataset consists of 7,787 non-diagram, multiple-choice science questions drawn from a variety of sources. Questions were partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set based on whether two baseline solvers, an information retrieval solver and a pointwise mutual information solver, answered them incorrectly. In addition, the ARC Corpus was created by using a major search engine to run a large series of science-relevant queries automatically constructed from about 100 hand-written templates for 80 science topics covered by US elementary and middle schools; top documents were collected, deduplicated, stripped to text, chunked into sentences, and augmented with the AristoMini corpus.
rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The question set contains natural science questions authored for use on standardized tests and drawn from a variety of sources, including publicly releasable subsets of prior science challenge questions and multiple state and assessment sources listed in the appendix. The ARC Corpus raw data came from Web documents retrieved via a major search engine using automatically instantiated science-topic query templates, plus the AristoMini corpus containing Wiktionary definitions, Simple Wikipedia science articles, and additional science sentences collected from the Web.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were sorted into a Challenge Set of 2,590 hard questions and an Easy Set of 5,197 questions. A Challenge question was operationally defined as one answered incorrectly by both the IR solver and the PMI solver. For the corpus, collected documents were de-duplicated, stripped down to text, and chunked into sentences, then augmented with the AristoMini corpus.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the ARC Corpus, queries were automatically constructed from hand-written templates and science-topic term lists; top documents from search results were collected and de-duplicated; document content was stripped down to just the text and chunked into sentences. In baseline entailment experiments, retrieved sentences were filtered to remove long sentences over 300 characters, sentences with negation, and noisy sentences.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset itself consists of standardized test questions with answer options and correct answers authored for human tests. No new human annotation process for the ARC questions is described. For analysis, the authors provide a categorization of knowledge and reasoning types based on a sample of 100 questions, noting that this requires subjective judgment. The paper also states that the Science Entailment dataset used to train some baseline models was created with crowdworkers annotating premises and hypotheses as entailing or not, but this is not annotation of ARC itself.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The categorization of knowledge and reasoning types shown for ARC is based on a sample of 100 questions, and the authors note that the relative sizes of categories are necessarily approximate because assigning the main challenge of a question requires subjective judgment.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The ARC Dataset, Corpus, three baseline neural models, and leaderboard are available at http://data.allenai.org/arc. The paper mentions an ARC leaderboard and says to access ARC, view the leaderboard, and submit new entries via the ARC website. No explicit versioning schedule, maintainers beyond Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, or deprecation policy is provided.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Questions vary in target student grade level, ranging from 3rd grade to 9th, corresponding to students typically of age 8 through 13 years.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to encourage AI research on more advanced question answering requiring reasoning, commonsense knowledge, and deeper text comprehension, rather than surface-level retrieval. The authors frame progress on ARC as a significant step forward for the community.
rai:dataBiases: The authors note that because standardized tests were designed for people rather than machines, large portions of such tests can be easily solved by simple AI methods, causing scores to be dominated by simple algorithms and biasing research toward incremental improvements in retrieval and statistical correlation methods rather than larger AI challenges. ARC addresses this by creating a Challenge partition. They also note that category analyses of knowledge and reasoning types are approximate and subjective.
rai:dataLimitations: The operational definition of Challenge questions as those missed by both IR and PMI only approximates the informal goal of identifying hard questions. The ARC Corpus has about 75% science-relevant documents in an informal sample, and while it appears to mention knowledge relevant to about 95% of Challenge questions, exploiting that knowledge is not trivial. The paper also notes that simple retrieval methods are biased toward sentences very similar to the question and away from sets of sentences that together explain the answer. Use of the corpus is optional, and systems are not restricted to it.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is presented as a challenge for advanced question answering research and benchmarking. It includes train, development, and test partitions for both the Challenge and Easy sets, and is used in the paper for evaluating baseline QA systems. The ARC Corpus is released as optional supporting text for corpus-based approaches; systems are not restricted to using it.
